title: These divisions match the scholastic pair, yet the Reformed fault it
source_text: VIII. Istae vero donorum gratiae divisiones apud Reformatos receptae parum aut nihil differunt a solenni apud Scholasticos gratiae divisione in gratiam gratis datam & gratiam gratum facientem: ut agnoscit Tilenus ante citata disputatione prima de variis divinae voluntatis nominibus thesi 22. Sed tamen Theologi Reformati plerique istam Scholae Romanae distinctionem carpunt & reprehendunt. Et primo quidem iis displicet quod quaedam Dei dona specialiter dicantur gratia gratis data: quia nulla est gratia quae non gratis donetur. Nec minus gratuita Dei dona sunt spes, fides & charitas, quam donum prophetiae, sanationum & similia.
pass_a_gloss: VIII. But these divisions of the gifts of grace received among the Reformed differ little or nothing from the solemn division among the Scholastics of grace into grace freely given and grace making pleasing: as Tilenus acknowledges in the before cited first disputation on the various names of the divine will thesis 22. But yet most Reformed Theologians carp at and reprehend that distinction of the Roman School. And first indeed it displeases them that certain gifts of God are specially called grace freely given: because there is no grace which is not given freely. Nor are hope, faith and charity less free gifts of God, than the gift of prophecy, of healings and the like.
pass_b_english: Thesis VIII. These divisions of the gifts of grace accepted among the Reformed differ little or not at all from the scholastics' standard division of grace into grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing. Tilenus admits as much in thesis 22 of the first disputation on the various names of the divine will, cited above.

Even so, most Reformed theologians criticize and find fault with this distinction of the Roman school. First, they object that some of God's gifts are singled out and called grace freely given, since there is no grace that is not given freely. Hope, faith and love are no less God's free gifts than the gift of prophecy, of healing and the like.

choices.why: The scholastic pair (Aquinas, Summa theologiae I-II q. 111 a. 1): gifts given for the good of others versus the grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God. Kept literal because the Reformed objections turn on the very words.
